# Exercise 4.3 — Choosing a threshold {#sec-thresholds}

**45 minutes · work individually, discuss Task 3 in pairs**

## Objectives

::: {.objective-list}
- Turn predicted probabilities into predicted classes at a stated threshold, and
  build the confusion table that results.
- Say what moving the threshold from 0.5 to 0.3 buys and what it costs, in
  patients rather than in percentages.
- Choose a threshold from a stated cost ratio, and defend the choice against the
  threshold that maximises accuracy.
:::

## Why this, here

@sec-logistic-regression ended with a probability of 0.302 for a patient with a
glucose of 120. No clinic can act on 0.302. Somebody has to decide whether that
patient is investigated further, and that decision needs a cut-off.

The cut-off is not part of the model. Nothing in the fitting procedure chose
0.5, no diagnostic accuracy study supports it, and the software offers it as a
default only because it has to offer something. Choosing it properly requires
one piece of information the data does not contain: what it costs to be wrong in
each of the two directions. In diabetes screening those costs are not remotely
equal — a missed diagnosis is years of untreated hyperglycaemia, a false alarm
is a fasting glucose test and a worried afternoon — and the whole of this
exercise follows from that asymmetry.

## Fit on the training rows, predict on the held-out ones

Same split as @sec-frameworks: every fifth row held back, so that the two
languages are working on the same 153 patients. This time we are making a claim
about unseen patients, so the split is doing real work.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
library(readr); library(dplyr); library(tidymodels)

diabetes <- read_csv("data/diabetes.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(diabetes = factor(diabetes, levels = c("neg", "pos")))

test_rows <- seq(5, nrow(diabetes), by = 5)
train <- diabetes[-test_rows, ]
test  <- diabetes[ test_rows, ]

fit <- logistic_reg() |> set_engine("glm") |> fit(diabetes ~ glucose, data = train)

preds <- predict(fit, test, type = "prob") |>
  bind_cols(test |> select(glucose, diabetes))

round(coef(fit$fit), 6)
c(n_test = nrow(test), pos = sum(test$diabetes == "pos"),
  neg = sum(test$diabetes == "neg"))
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np, pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

diabetes = pd.read_csv("data/diabetes.csv")
is_test = (diabetes.index + 1) % 5 == 0
train, test = diabetes[~is_test], diabetes[is_test]

y_train = (train["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)
y_test  = (test["diabetes"] == "pos").astype(int)

fit = LogisticRegression(C=np.inf, max_iter=1000).fit(train[["glucose"]], y_train)
p_pos = fit.predict_proba(test[["glucose"]])[:, 1]

print(round(fit.intercept_[0], 6), round(fit.coef_[0][0], 6))
print(len(test), int(y_test.sum()), int((y_test == 0).sum()))
```
:::

Both languages fit the same model to the same 615 patients and report an
intercept of −5.308065 and a glucose coefficient of 0.037362. The test set is
153 patients, 55 of them `pos`. Every number below is therefore directly
comparable between the two tabs, which was the point of fixing the split.

The predicted probabilities run from 0.078 to 0.874 and average 0.386.

## A threshold is a rule, and a rule has consequences

```{r}
#| fig-height: 3.4
library(ggplot2)
ggplot(preds, aes(x = glucose, y = .pred_pos, colour = diabetes)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.7, size = 1.6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Glucose (mg/dL)", y = "Predicted P(pos)", colour = NULL,
       caption = "Dashed lines: thresholds 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7")
```

Everything above a line is called positive, everything below it negative. With
one predictor the picture is unusually honest: a probability threshold *is* a
glucose cut-off, and these three are 119, 142 and 165 mg/dL. Any colour above a
line that is not the positive class is a false alarm; any positive-class point
below it is a missed diagnosis.

## Task 1 — Three thresholds, three confusion tables

Count the four cells of the confusion table at 0.3, 0.5 and 0.7, and turn them
into sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value. Do it by counting
first: the packaged functions come in the next section, and they are much easier
to misuse than to use.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
counts <- function(threshold) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= ______
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  tibble(threshold = threshold,
         TP = sum(called_pos & truly_pos),
         FP = sum(called_pos & !truly_pos),
         FN = sum(!called_pos & ______),
         TN = sum(!called_pos & !truly_pos))
}

bind_rows(lapply(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), counts)) |>
  mutate(sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN),
         specificity = TN / (TN + FP),
         ppv         = TP / (TP + FP),
         accuracy    = (TP + TN) / nrow(preds))
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
counts <- function(threshold) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  tibble(threshold = threshold,
         TP = sum(called_pos & truly_pos),
         FP = sum(called_pos & !truly_pos),
         FN = sum(!called_pos & truly_pos),
         TN = sum(!called_pos & !truly_pos))
}

threshold_table <- bind_rows(lapply(c(0.3, 0.5, 0.7), counts)) |>
  mutate(sensitivity = TP / (TP + FN),
         specificity = TN / (TN + FP),
         ppv         = TP / (TP + FP),
         accuracy    = (TP + TN) / nrow(preds))
threshold_table
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
rows = []
for threshold in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
    called_pos = p_pos >= ______
    truly_pos  = y_test.to_numpy() == 1
    tp = int(( called_pos &  truly_pos).sum())
    fp = int(( called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())
    fn = int((~called_pos &  ______).sum())
    tn = int((~called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())
    rows.append(dict(threshold=threshold, TP=tp, FP=fp, FN=fn, TN=tn,
                     sensitivity=tp / (tp + fn), specificity=tn / (tn + fp),
                     ppv=tp / (tp + fp), accuracy=(tp + tn) / len(y_test)))
pd.DataFrame(rows).round(3)
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
rows = []
for threshold in [0.3, 0.5, 0.7]:
    called_pos = p_pos >= threshold
    truly_pos  = y_test.to_numpy() == 1
    tp = int(( called_pos &  truly_pos).sum())
    fp = int(( called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())
    fn = int((~called_pos &  truly_pos).sum())
    tn = int((~called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum())
    rows.append(dict(threshold=threshold, TP=tp, FP=fp, FN=fn, TN=tn,
                     sensitivity=tp / (tp + fn), specificity=tn / (tn + fp),
                     ppv=tp / (tp + fp), accuracy=(tp + tn) / len(y_test)))
threshold_table = pd.DataFrame(rows)
threshold_table.round(3)
```
:::
:::
:::

You should get, in both languages:

| Threshold | TP | FP | FN | TN | Sensitivity | Specificity | PPV | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0.3 | 42 | 38 | 13 | 60 | 0.764 | 0.612 | 0.525 | 0.667 |
| 0.5 | 25 | 15 | 30 | 83 | 0.455 | 0.847 | 0.625 | 0.706 |
| 0.7 | 17 | 11 | 38 | 87 | 0.309 | 0.888 | 0.607 | 0.680 |

: {tbl-colwidths="[13,8,8,8,8,15,15,12,13]"}

Read the FN column before anything else. At the default threshold the model
misses 30 of the 55 patients who have diabetes. At 0.7 it misses 38 — more than
two in three. Moving from 0.5 down to 0.3 finds 17 more of them and raises the
false alarms from 15 to 38.

## The packaged version, and the trap in it

Both languages ship a confusion-matrix function, and both have a convention
about which class counts as the event. Getting it wrong silently swaps your
sensitivity and your specificity.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
preds_0.5 <- preds |>
  mutate(predicted = factor(if_else(.pred_pos >= 0.5, "pos", "neg"),
                            levels = c("neg", "pos")))

conf_mat(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted)

c(default      = sens(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted)$.estimate,
  event_second = sens(preds_0.5, truth = diabetes, estimate = predicted,
                      event_level = "second")$.estimate)
```

## Python

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, recall_score

print(confusion_matrix(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int), labels=[0, 1]))

{"pos_label=1": round(recall_score(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int)), 3),
 "pos_label=0": round(recall_score(y_test, (p_pos >= 0.5).astype(int), pos_label=0), 3)}
```
:::

`yardstick` treats the **first** factor level as the event, and our levels are
`neg, pos`, so its default sensitivity of 0.847 is the specificity of the thing
you care about. `event_level = "second"` recovers 0.455. scikit-learn makes the
same decision with `pos_label`, which defaults to 1 and therefore happens to be
right here — but only because we coded the outcome as 0/1 in that order.

The original course notes for this material converted the outcome to a 0/1
factor before calling `conf_mat()`, which made `"0"` the first level and the
event. The table they printed was a correct table of the wrong event. It is a
one-word fault, it does not raise an error, and the numbers it produces are
plausible — which is the whole problem.

## Task 2 — Put a price on the two errors

A missed diagnosis is not a false alarm. For this exercise, take a missed case
to cost **five times** what a false alarm costs — the ratio is a decision for a
service, not a statistician, and Task 3 asks you to argue with it.

Compute the total cost over a grid of thresholds, find the cheapest one, and
compare it with two strategies that use no model at all: investigate everybody,
and investigate nobody.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
cost_of <- function(threshold, cost_fn = 5, cost_fp = 1) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  cost_fn * sum(______ & truly_pos) + cost_fp * sum(called_pos & !truly_pos)
}

grid <- tibble(threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(cost = sapply(threshold, cost_of))

best <- grid |> slice_min(cost, n = 1)
c(best_threshold = best$threshold, best_cost = best$cost,
  cost_at_0.5    = cost_of(0.5),
  investigate_everyone = cost_of(______),
  investigate_nobody   = cost_of(1.01))
```

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Stuck?
"Investigate everybody" is not a special case needing its own code: it is the
rule you get from a threshold low enough that every predicted probability clears
it. The lowest probability in the test set is 0.078.
:::

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
cost_of <- function(threshold, cost_fn = 5, cost_fp = 1) {
  called_pos <- preds$.pred_pos >= threshold
  truly_pos  <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  cost_fn * sum(!called_pos & truly_pos) + cost_fp * sum(called_pos & !truly_pos)
}

grid <- tibble(threshold = seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)) |>
  mutate(cost = sapply(threshold, cost_of))

best <- grid |> slice_min(cost, n = 1)
c(best_threshold = best$threshold, best_cost = best$cost,
  cost_at_0.5    = cost_of(0.5),
  investigate_everyone = cost_of(0),
  investigate_nobody   = cost_of(1.01))
```
:::
:::

## Python

```{python}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
truly_pos = y_test.to_numpy() == 1

def cost_of(threshold, cost_fn=5, cost_fp=1):
    called_pos = p_pos >= threshold
    return cost_fn * (______ & truly_pos).sum() + cost_fp * (called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum()

grid = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
costs = np.array([cost_of(t) for t in grid])

{"best_threshold": float(grid[costs.argmin()]), "best_cost": int(costs.min()),
 "cost_at_0.5": int(cost_of(0.5)),
 "investigate_everyone": int(cost_of(______)), "investigate_nobody": int(cost_of(1.01))}
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{python}
truly_pos = y_test.to_numpy() == 1

def cost_of(threshold, cost_fn=5, cost_fp=1):
    called_pos = p_pos >= threshold
    return cost_fn * (~called_pos & truly_pos).sum() + cost_fp * (called_pos & ~truly_pos).sum()

grid = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
costs = np.array([cost_of(t) for t in grid])

{"best_threshold": float(grid[costs.argmin()]), "best_cost": int(costs.min()),
 "cost_at_0.5": int(cost_of(0.5)),
 "investigate_everyone": int(cost_of(0)), "investigate_nobody": int(cost_of(1.01))}
```
:::
:::
:::

## The result that should bother you

The default threshold is not merely suboptimal here. It is beaten by a policy
with no model in it.

1. At 0.5 the model's accuracy is 0.706, against 0.641 for always saying `neg`.
   Six and a half percentage points for three decades of diabetes research, and
   a student reporting only accuracy would call that a working classifier.
2. At 0.5 the same model misses 30 of 55 cases. Those two sentences describe the
   same 153 patients. Accuracy is high because the model is good at the common
   class, and the common class is the one nobody is screening for.
3. Price the errors at 5:1 and the arithmetic turns hostile. The default
   threshold costs 165. Investigating **every** one of the 153 patients costs 98,
   because it incurs 98 false alarms and no missed cases. The model as deployed
   at its default is two-thirds worse than a policy that ignores it.

The model is not useless: at its cost-minimising threshold of 0.17 it costs 74,
about a quarter less than investigating everybody. But that is the honest size of
the win, it arrives only once somebody states the cost ratio, and it is invisible
at 0.5.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Where 0.17 comes from
For a known cost ratio the optimal threshold is
$\text{cost}_{FP} / (\text{cost}_{FP} + \text{cost}_{FN})$ — here
$1/(1+5) = 0.167$ — whenever the predicted probabilities are well calibrated.
Our grid finds 0.17 empirically on 153 patients, which is agreement to the
nearest grid point and partly luck. The theoretical result is the thing to
remember; the grid is what you run when you do not trust the calibration, which
is most of the time.
:::

## Task 3 — Set the operating point, and defend it

Find the highest threshold at which sensitivity is at least 0.80, then report
what it costs. Write two sentences for a diabetes service: one stating the rule
in glucose rather than in probability, one stating the price.

::: {.panel-tabset}
## R

```{r}
#| eval: false
# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
source("checks/checks.R")
sens_at <- function(t) {
  truly_pos <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t & truly_pos) / sum(truly_pos)
}
candidates <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
chosen <- max(candidates[sapply(candidates, sens_at) >= ______])

ppv_at <- function(t) sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t & preds$diabetes == "pos") /
                      sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t)
c(threshold = chosen, sensitivity = sens_at(chosen), ppv = ppv_at(chosen))
check_metric_range(sens_at(chosen), 0.80, 1.00, "sensitivity at the chosen threshold")
```

::: {.content-visible when-meta="show-solutions"}
::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Worked answer
```{r}
source("checks/checks.R")
sens_at <- function(t) {
  truly_pos <- preds$diabetes == "pos"
  sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t & truly_pos) / sum(truly_pos)
}
candidates <- seq(0.01, 0.99, by = 0.01)
chosen <- max(candidates[sapply(candidates, sens_at) >= 0.80])

ppv_at <- function(t) sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t & preds$diabetes == "pos") /
                      sum(preds$.pred_pos >= t)
c(threshold = chosen, sensitivity = sens_at(chosen), ppv = ppv_at(chosen))
check_metric_range(sens_at(chosen), 0.80, 1.00, "sensitivity at the chosen threshold")
```
:::
:::

## Worked answer
```{python}
import sys; sys.path.append("checks")
from checks import *

def sens_at(t):
    return ((p_pos >= t) & truly_pos).sum() / truly_pos.sum()

def ppv_at(t):
    return ((p_pos >= t) & truly_pos).sum() / (p_pos >= t).sum()

candidates = np.round(np.arange(0.01, 1.00, 0.01), 2)
chosen = max(t for t in candidates if sens_at(t) >= 0.80)

print({"threshold": chosen, "sensitivity": round(sens_at(chosen), 3),

check_metric_range(sens_at(chosen), 0.80, 1.00, "sensitivity at the chosen threshold")
```
:::
:::
:::

The answer is 0.28, which catches 44 of the 55 cases and raises 43 false alarms.
Its positive predictive value is 0.506: **half the people this rule sends for
investigation do not have diabetes**, and its accuracy, 0.647, is almost exactly
the do-nothing baseline. A service can accept that — screening programmes
routinely do — but only if someone has said so out loud. Write the two
sentences before you look at the next section.

## Reflection

1. Sensitivity rose from 0.455 to 0.800 and accuracy fell from 0.706 to 0.647.
   Explain to a sceptical colleague why that is an improvement, without using
   the word "cost".
2. Everything here was computed on 153 patients with the prevalence this file
   happens to have. Name one thing that changes about your chosen threshold if
   the model is deployed in a population where diabetes is half as common, and
   say which of the four numbers in the confusion table move first.

::: {.content-visible when-profile="instructor"}
::: {.instructor}
**Expected values** (the data is synthetic; the last digit may move if it is
regenerated). Train 615, test 153 with 55 `pos`. Coefficients: intercept
≈ −5.308, glucose ≈ 0.0374, identical in both languages because the split is
fixed. Confusion tables as printed in the table above. Majority-class accuracy
0.641. Costs at 5:1 — threshold 0.5: 165; 0.3: 103; 0.7: 201; best threshold
0.17 at 74; investigate everybody 98; investigate nobody 275. Operating point
for sensitivity ≥ 0.80: threshold 0.28, sensitivity 0.800, PPV 0.506, accuracy
0.647.

**Answers.** (1) The two errors are different events with different
consequences, and accuracy is the one summary that insists they are the same;
an improvement that trades 15 false alarms for 19 found cases is an improvement
in everything except the metric that cannot tell them apart. (2) Prevalence does
not change sensitivity or specificity, which are conditional on the truth, but
it does change PPV, which falls — so the same threshold produces a far worse
false-alarm rate in a lower-prevalence population. TP and FN fall together; FP
and TN rise. This is the single most common reason a published screening model
disappoints on deployment, and it connects straight back to @sec-shift.

**Plenary.** Ask for the Task 3 sentences aloud from two or three people. The
useful disagreement is about the 5:1 ratio; a diabetes service might argue for
10:1, an over-stretched endoscopy list for 2:1, and the point is that the number
is theirs and not ours. Nobody should leave thinking 0.17 is a property of the
model.

**Common failures.** (1) Computing the cost with the FN and FP terms swapped —
it produces a cost-minimising threshold near 0.9, which is the tell. (2)
Comparing a threshold chosen on the test set with a score on the same test set:
say out loud that the 0.17 is itself fitted, and that a defensible pipeline
chooses the threshold on a validation split. (3) `preds$.pred_pos >= 0.5`
written with `>`; with 153 continuous probabilities it changes nothing, and it
is worth asking when it would.

**Timing.** Task 1 and the result-that-should-bother-you are the day. Task 2 can
be shortened to the three thresholds already in the table if the room is slow;
Task 3 can go home.
:::
:::

## Stretch

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 1 — All the thresholds at once
Plot sensitivity against 1 − specificity across the whole grid. You have just
drawn a ROC curve by hand, and the area under it is the one classification
summary that does not depend on the threshold — which is a virtue and a vice.
@sec-classification-metrics is the full treatment; arriving there having built
the curve from counts is worth an hour of slides.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 2 — Choose the threshold honestly
Split the 615 training rows again into fit and validation parts, choose the
threshold on the validation part, and only then report its cost on the test set.
Does the cost go up? It usually does, and the gap is the price of having chosen
the threshold on the data you then reported.
:::

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
## Stretch 3 — Does a better model move the threshold?
Refit with `diabetes ~ glucose + mass + age` and repeat Task 2. The cost at the
best threshold falls; ask whether the best threshold itself moved, and whether
you would have predicted the direction.
:::

## What you can and cannot now claim

**Can:** that at a stated threshold, on 153 held-out patients, this model finds a
stated fraction of the diabetes in them at a stated false-alarm rate — and that
you can produce the threshold a stated cost ratio implies.

**Cannot:** that any of these thresholds is right for a real service. The cost
ratio was invented for the exercise, the prevalence is this file's, the
probabilities have not been checked for calibration, and the threshold was
chosen on the same rows it was scored on. Each of those is a day of its own, and
@sec-classification-metrics is the next one.
